snippets.output: In this 55-year-old male with right arm weakness, dull aching and burning right arm pain, decreased sensation in the right arm, and a smoking history of 2 packs per day since age 25, the most likely diagnosis is an apical lung tumor, also known as a Pancoast tumor. A Pancoast tumor can involve the brachial plexus, causing arm weakness, pain, and sensory changes, and is often associated with smoking.

Brachial plexopathy can present with weakness and sensory loss, but in this 55-year-old male with right arm weakness and sensory loss over a few weeks, brachial plexopathy is less likely because it is typically not chronic and progressive without an identifiable cause such as trauma.

Cerebral infarction is a possible diagnosis because cerebral infarction can cause sudden-onset weakness and typically presents with other neurological deficits such as facial droop; however, in this 55-year-old male with gradually progressive right arm weakness over weeks, cerebral infarction is less likely.

Scalenus anticus syndrome is a variant of thoracic outlet syndrome and is usually exacerbated by neck movements or arm positioning. In this 55-year-old male with right arm weakness, decreased sensation, and dull aching and burning right arm pain, symptoms are unchanged with head and neck position, making scalenus anticus syndrome less likely.
Subclavian steal syndrome is a possible diagnosis; subclavian steal syndrome presents with arm claudication and neurologic symptoms due to blood flow reversal and typically worsens with arm exertion.

In this 55-year-old male with a heavy smoking history, progressive right arm weakness, dull aching and burning right arm pain, and decreased sensation in the right arm, the most likely diagnosis is an apical lung tumor (Pancoast tumor). An apical lung tumor fits this clinical picture because it can involve the brachial plexus, causing the described weakness, pain, and sensory changes.
